newsitem.title: GERMANY: Scientology criticises Germany for new measures.
newsitem.headline: Scientology criticises Germany for new measures.

text.p: The Church of Scientology lashed out against German federal and state governments on Friday for a series of measures taken to counter the organisation.
"It feels like religious cleansing," the Church of Scientolgy Germany said in a statement. "It feels as if they want to take away German citizenship from those who think differently."
Germany's federal and regional governments agreed a package of steps on Wednesday to counter what they called the "expansionist aims and claim to domination" of the Church of Scientology.

The move aimed to establish a unified approach against the U.S.-based group after a number of politicians and regional states called for action against what they consider to be a profit-making, pseudo-religious sect relying on manipulation.
Authorities also agreed to consider putting Scientology under surveillance by the anti-extremist Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV).
But the Munich-based Church said it would challenge the state's actions in court.
"In the interest of democracy in our country, the Scientology members will take legal action against this totalitarian trend," a Church of Scientology spokesman said.
In the past year, Scientology has drawn fire from several quarters in Germany, especially the state of Bavaria and Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats.

Bonn has published a booklet warning of the what it says are the dangers of the organisation and Bavaria is making state employees fill out a questionnaire detailing their ties to the group. It has called for Scientologists to be banned from public service.
The governments also agreed to exclude Scientologists as far as legally possible from public contracts for installations requiring a special degree of trust, such as education and advice centres.

Germany has stricter regulations on church status than the United States and has refused to register Scientology as a religion. The group says it has around 30,000 members in Germany though the government puts the figure between 10,000 and 20,000.
